summary: Year 3 children (age 7–8) learn to read an analogue clock to the nearest minute AND build a felt sense of how long seconds, minutes and hours actually are — estimating real durations, comparing them, and choosing sensible units for events. The hard parts are: estimating (children tend to count seconds in their head far too fast, so estimates come out wildly short), comparing (they compare bare numbers while ignoring units, e.g. '30 seconds is longer than 20 minutes because 30 > 20'), and selecting an appropriate unit for an event. Precise reading should be paired with hands-on calibration against a real timer and with comparisons laid out in a common unit.
misconceptions: Counts seconds in the head too quickly, so estimates are badly short
Compares numbers without reference to units (30 seconds > 20 minutes because 30 > 20)
Chooses the wrong unit for an event (seconds for a lesson, hours for a blink)
Thinks a later finish time means a longer duration (carried from earlier duration confusion)
Reads to the nearest minute by counting single minutes from the 12

activities.title: Tap when you think the time has passed — then reveal the real elapsed time
steps: Close your eyes (or watch a blank screen) and tap/raise a hand when you think 30 seconds has passed.
Compare the moment you tapped with the real elapsed time measured on a stopwatch or timer.
Notice the gap between your tap and the real time — many children tap early for a 30-second estimate because they count too fast in their head, so check whether that happened for you.
Try again, practising a steady 'one-Mississippi' counting pace, and re-estimate to see if your tap gets closer.
Repeat for a minute and for 40 seconds.
activities.insight: My internal counting can run faster than real seconds; estimating duration is a felt skill I can calibrate against a real timer by checking my tap against the measured time.

activities.title: Compare two durations on one common-unit scale
steps: Take two durations, '30 seconds' and '20 minutes', and place them as bars onto ONE shared number line marked in a common unit (e.g. seconds).
See that 20 minutes = 1200 seconds towers over the 30-second sliver.
State which is longer and say WHY: a minute is 60 seconds, so 20 minutes is 1200 seconds, which is longer than 30 seconds even though 20 is less than 30.
Try more pairs, including a tricky one: 90 seconds vs 2 minutes (90 > 2, but 90s < 120s, so 2 minutes is longer).
activities.insight: Durations can only be compared fairly when expressed in the same unit; the bare number alone does not tell you which is longer.

activities.title: Read an analogue clock to the exact minute by counting on from the last five
steps: Look at a clock showing 2:38.
Find which five the minute hand has just passed (the 35).
Count on from there to the exact minute (+3 to reach 38).
Read the time to the nearest minute and explain the counting-on method.
Rehearse with the five-minute marks shown on the clock face.
activities.insight: Reading to the exact minute is efficient when I anchor on the last five and count on, rather than counting single minutes from the 12.

activities.title: Match events to sensible units using benchmarks
steps: Anchor each unit to a familiar benchmark: a second ≈ one clap, a minute ≈ a short song, an hour ≈ a lesson.
Sort everyday events against these benchmarks (a blink, brushing teeth, eating lunch, sleeping overnight).
Choose whether each event is best measured in seconds, minutes or hours, and justify by comparing to the benchmark.
Catch mismatches such as 'lunch takes 30 seconds' or 'a blink takes hours'.
activities.insight: Each unit has a felt size; I pick the unit for an event by comparing it to a benchmark I know.

activities.title: Sequence and compare durations
steps: Put a set of durations in order from shortest to longest: 90 seconds, 1 minute, 1 hour, 2 minutes (correct order: 1 minute, 90 seconds, 2 minutes, 1 hour).
Answer 'which is longer, 30 seconds or 20 minutes?' and explain the reasoning in units.
Match a list of events to their natural unit.
Estimate how long brushing teeth takes using a slider or spoken estimate, then check against a timer.
activities.insight: I can order and compare durations reliably by converting to a common unit and reasoning about unit size.

checkQuestion: Set estimating, reading and comparing tasks and WATCH: (1) Analogue clock at 2:38: 'Read this to the nearest minute and show me how.' (2) 'Close your eyes and put your hand up when you think 30 seconds has gone' — time it. (3) 'Which is longer — 30 seconds or 20 minutes? How do you know?' and 'About how long does it take to eat lunch — seconds, minutes or hours?' Watch the reading method, how far off the estimate is, and whether they reason about UNITS rather than just the numbers.
checkAnswer: Reads 2:38 by counting on from 35 (+3); estimates 30 seconds within a sensible range (not tapping at around 10 seconds); says 20 minutes is longer than 30 seconds BECAUSE minutes are bigger units (converting or reasoning about unit size); picks minutes for lunch.
